strengths: Identifies and clearly motivates a real, underexplored problem in open-vocabulary 3DSG pipelines: noise propagation from occluded/constrained-viewpoint object crops into cross-image aggregation, illustrated convincingly with qualitative examples (Fig. 1, Fig. 6).

The re-shot guided uncertainty estimation is a reasonably novel idea: rendering an occlusion-free, best-view image from the reconstructed object point cloud and comparing its caption against crop captions provides a principled proxy for caption reliability without requiring extra supervision.

Dynamic downsample-mapping strategy is simple but effective, yielding a substantial (~2.7x) speedup in 3D object mapping while maintaining comparable closed-set segmentation accuracy (Table 2), addressing a genuine bottleneck in existing pipelines (e.g., ConceptGraphs).

Comprehensive ablation study (Fig. 3, Fig. 5) isolates the contribution of re-shot uncertainty estimation, RAG-based refinement, random-vs-semantic retrieval, and concatenated re-shot prompts, with results consistently supporting the design choices.
Human-evaluated node/edge precision results show a clear and consistent improvement over ConceptGraphs/ConceptGraphs-Detector baselines across all 8 Replica scenes (Table 1), not just in aggregate.
Paper is generally clearly written, with a well-illustrated pipeline diagram and appendix materials (pseudo-code, dynamic voxel-size examples, re-shot visualizations) that aid reproducibility.
weaknesses: Evaluation is confined to a single, relatively small and synthetic dataset (Replica, 8 scenes); no results on more diverse/realistic environments (e.g., ScanNet, real-world RGB-D captures) to demonstrate generalization beyond a controlled benchmark.

Baseline comparison is narrow: only ConceptGraphs and ConceptGraphs-Detector are directly compared in Table 1/2, while other open-vocabulary 3DSG methods discussed in Related Work (Open3DSG, Clio, HOV-SG) are omitted from the main node/edge precision comparison, weakening the strength of the claimed superiority.

The claimed 'comparable or superior' closed-set segmentation accuracy in Table 2 is a wash: mAcc is only marginally better (40.67 vs 40.63) and f-mIoU is actually slightly worse than ConceptGraphs (35.65 vs 35.95), so the framing somewhat overstates the result; the real contribution here is speed, which should be foregrounded more honestly.

Human evaluation protocol lacks important methodological details: number of annotators, inter-annotator agreement, and whether annotators were blind to method identity are not reported, making the significance of the precision gains harder to assess.

The 'RAG' terminology is a loose analogy to LLM-RAG; in practice it is a simple nearest-neighbor context retrieval of one adjacent object's caption, which is a reasonable but relatively modest technical contribution rather than a novel retrieval mechanism.

No analysis of the added computational/API cost from re-shot rendering, extra VLM calls, and clustering steps—these could partially offset the touted mapping-time savings, but end-to-end runtime with all components is not reported.

Heavy reliance on proprietary API models (GPT-4, GPT-4o-mini) for core pipeline stages raises reproducibility concerns (cost, model drift/versioning) despite the reproducibility statement; only a single alternative VLM (LLaVA) is tested in one anecdotal appendix case rather than systematically.

strengths: The core idea of 'active re-shooting'—rendering a synthetic optimal-viewpoint image from the fused 3D point cloud and comparing its caption against passive multi-view crop captions—is a novel and intuitive way to quantify per-object semantic uncertainty in open-vocabulary 3DSG pipelines, moving beyond passive best-frame selection used in prior work (BBQ, MomaGraph).

The evaluation is unusually comprehensive for this subfield: automated Recall@K on two real-world benchmarks (SceneFun3D, FunGraph3D), a carefully designed human evaluation on Replica with inter-annotator agreement (Fleiss' kappa = 0.76), a dedicated ablation study isolating the contribution of the re-shot module, RAG, and image concatenation, an explicit stress test with injected pose noise, and a real-world robot deployment.

Reported gains over strong baselines (OpenFunGraph, ConceptGraphs, Open3DSG) are consistent and often substantial, both in automated recall metrics and human-judged precision/duplicate-reduction, lending credibility to the claimed improvements.

The method is designed with practical deployment in mind: it offers both an open-source (LLaVA) and proprietary (GPT-4o) variant, reports runtime/cost figures, and discusses integration into online robotic architectures, which strengthens the paper's relevance to the Applied/Systems aspect of the contribution.

The dynamic voxel-size downsampling and dynamic NN-ratio thresholding are reasonable, well-motivated engineering choices that are shown (via runtime numbers) to meaningfully accelerate the fusion stage relative to ConceptGraphs.
weaknesses: The technical novelty is largely a clever combination of existing components (view-quality scoring, CLIP similarity clustering, nearest-neighbor retrieval, VLM prompting) rather than a fundamentally new algorithmic contribution; the 'RAG' module is a simple spatial nearest-neighbor context lookup rather than a learned or dense retrieval mechanism, which may be an overstatement of the RAG framing.

Key implementation details of the re-shot rendering process (e.g., how textured/colored renders are produced from a possibly sparse and incomplete fused point cloud, and how rendering artifacts are handled) are not clearly specified in the main text, raising reproducibility concerns.

The paper does not quantitatively compare against several recent and directly relevant open-vocabulary 3DSG baselines discussed in the related work (e.g., BBQ, Clio, MomaGraph), limiting the strength of the SOTA claim to only three baselines.

Important hyperparameters (e.g., the top-50% threshold for low- vs. high-uncertainty partitioning, scoring weights αvis/αhoriz/αprior) appear to be fixed without sensitivity analysis in the main paper, and their robustness/generality across scenes is unclear.

The real-world robotic deployment section is purely qualitative/descriptive (no quantitative metrics reported for the robot trial), which weakens the empirical support for the robotic-readiness claims made in the abstract and conclusion.

The pipeline is inherently multi-stage and reliant on several foundation models (SAM, CLIP, GPT-4o/LLaVA) at multiple points, which could compound latency, cost, and error propagation in practice; while runtime is reported, the system remains offline and the online extension is only speculative.

The ablation figures (Fig. 3) use a different metric set (mIoU, mRecall, f-mIoU, etc.) computed via a distinct GT-matching procedure than the main Recall@K tables, making it harder to directly connect ablation conclusions to the main results.

strengths: The core motivation is intuitive and well-illustrated: passive per-view captioning under occlusion/constrained viewpoints introduces label noise (e.g., 'vase' mistakenly assigned to a table), and the paper proposes a concrete mechanism (virtual re-shooting from reconstructed geometry) to actively verify rather than passively select among existing views.

The evaluation is broad: two real-world benchmarks with standard Recall@K protocols (following OpenFunGraph), a carefully designed human evaluation on Replica with inter-annotator agreement (Fleiss' kappa) reported, an ablation study isolating the contribution of re-shot uncertainty estimation, RAG, and image concatenation, an injected-pose-noise stress test, and a real robotic deployment—together forming a reasonably complete validation package for a systems-oriented contribution.

Reporting both a GPT-4o variant and a locally-deployable LLaVA variant is a useful practical consideration, showing that the proposed diagnose-then-rectify pipeline provides gains even with a weaker open-source VLM.
The dynamic-downsampling strategy and threshold-scaled edge construction are simple, well-motivated engineering choices that measurably reduce runtime relative to ConceptGraphs.
weaknesses: Despite extensively discussing frame-selection/active-viewpoint baselines in Related Work (BBQ, MomaGraph, Think3D, Chain-of-View), none of these are included as experimental baselines; the comparison set (Open3DSG, ConceptGraphs, OpenFunGraph) does not include the most conceptually relevant competitors, weakening the empirical case that 'active re-shooting' is actually superior to passive best-view selection strategies like BBQ's clustering approach.

The uncertainty estimation trusts the re-shot caption as a pseudo ground truth, but the re-shot itself depends on reconstructed point-cloud quality and a VLM's ability to interpret a synthetically rendered image; there is no direct validation that re-shot captions are more accurate than the best passive crop, only that they differ from noisy aggregates—this leaves open the possibility that the 'active verification' signal is itself sometimes unreliable, especially for small/thin/incompletely reconstructed objects.

Key hyperparameters (view-scoring weights αvis/αhoriz/αprior, similarity threshold δsim, top-50% cutoff for anchor selection) appear to be manually set without in-paper sensitivity analysis; the paper defers this to supplementary material not included here, making it hard to assess robustness of these design choices.

The improvements over the strongest baseline (OpenFunGraph) on the two main benchmarks are often modest (e.g., +2.4% R@10 on SceneFun3D objects, +3.9% R@10 on FunGraph3D objects), and some edge metrics show OpenFunGraph still competitive or better (e.g., Edge R@5 on SceneFun3D: 88.1 OpenFunGraph vs 86.2 Ours-GPT), somewhat undercutting the 'new state-of-the-art' framing.

The human evaluation, while methodologically sound, is limited to 8 scenes on a single clean synthetic-reconstruction dataset (Replica) and compares only against ConceptGraphs variants, not against OpenFunGraph, which is the strongest automated baseline—this is an inconsistency in which baseline is used for which evaluation.

Several claimed contributions ('first to address semantic inconsistency,' 'exceptional resilience') are strong rhetorical claims not fully substantiated by ablations isolating whether gains stem primarily from the re-shot mechanism versus simply from richer/better VLM prompting (concatenated crop+re-shot images), given that 'w/o Concat' already causes a sizeable performance drop independent of the uncertainty-estimation logic itself.

The paper's contribution is largely a systems-level integration of existing components (SAM segmentation, CLIP embeddings, VLM captioning, cosine-similarity-based clustering, RAG retrieval) rather than a fundamentally new algorithmic or theoretical advance; this is a legitimate contribution type but the manuscript does not explicitly frame itself this way, leading to some overclaiming of technical novelty relative to prior viewpoint-aware 3DSG work.

No analysis of failure cases or scenarios where the re-shot mechanism could mislead the system (e.g., heavily occluded objects where even optimal virtual viewpoints cannot recover missing geometry) is provided, despite this being a natural limitation of a method relying on reconstructed point-cloud completeness.

strengths: Well-motivated problem framing: existing open-vocabulary 3DSG pipelines aggregate noisy per-view captions without discrimination, and the paper clearly diagnoses this failure mode (occlusion, constrained viewpoints) with intuitive examples.

The core technical idea—actively 're-shooting' objects from optimal synthesized viewpoints using the fused 3D geometry to cross-check passive observations—is a reasonable and reasonably novel way to move from passive frame-selection (as in BBQ, MomaGraph) to active verification, and is clearly distinguished from prior work in the related-work section.

Extensive and varied empirical validation: quantitative benchmarks on SceneFun3D and FunGraph3D, fine-grained human evaluation with inter-annotator agreement (Fleiss' kappa) on Replica, an explicit noisy-pose stress test, and a real physical robot deployment with a custom sensor suite. This breadth of evidence (simulation + human eval + robustness + real hardware) is uncommon and strengthens claims of practical readiness.

Thorough ablation studies isolating the contribution of re-shot uncertainty estimation, RAG, image concatenation, and random retrieval, plus supplementary hyperparameter sweeps (voxel size, merge threshold, scoring weights, retrieval top-k) that support the chosen default configuration with quantitative and qualitative (failure-case) justification.

Good reproducibility support: detailed prompts, pseudo-code for the incremental fusion algorithm, and runtime/cost analysis (including consumer-GPU feasibility and per-scene API cost) are provided in the supplementary material.

Reasonable ablations showing that edge-level gains are largely inherited from improved node semantics (Ours Node + CG Edge), which is a useful mechanistic insight rather than just an aggregate score improvement.
weaknesses: The core contribution is a combination of existing ingredients (best-view/frame-selection strategies, embedding-similarity-based uncertainty, and retrieval-augmented generation) rather than a fundamentally new technique; each individual component (KMeans clustering with K=3, cosine-similarity uncertainty, position-based retrieval) is somewhat ad hoc and not theoretically grounded, and the novelty framing ("first to address...") is arguably overstated relative to related active-viewpoint reasoning works cited (Think3D, CoV, BBQ).

The re-shot rendering pipeline depends on point-cloud quality; the supplementary failure-case analysis (e.g., ceiling/door renders collapsing to unreadable lines, transparent/bright objects being miscaptioned as "white candle") suggests the re-shot signal itself can be unreliable, and the system's fallback (image concatenation with the best 2D crop) partially masks rather than resolves this brittleness—raising questions about how often re-shots are simply wrong versus genuinely diagnostic.

Evaluation potentially confounded by using GPT-4o as both a component of the proposed pipeline (captioning, refinement) and as the semantic assigner/evaluator in the ablation study (Sec 4.4), which could bias reported gains in favor of the GPT-based variant.

The robustness/noise experiments use fairly mild injected noise (σtrans=0.02m, σrot=1°); this does not clearly establish robustness under more severe tracking drift or degraded RGB-D sensing that is common in real deployments, despite claims of "profound resilience."

No variance/error bars or multiple-seed reporting for the quantitative Recall@K results or the real-robot precision numbers (e.g., 65.6% vs 83.8%), making it hard to assess the statistical significance of reported margins, some of which (e.g., 0.9% Object R@3 drop under noisy pose) are quite small.

Runtime/cost comparisons are informative but do not fully account for the substantially higher inference cost (multiple VLM calls per object for re-shot captioning, RAG refinement, and additional rendering) versus single-caption baselines like ConceptGraphs when interpreting the performance gap—an apples-to-apples cost-normalized comparison is missing.

The edge relation taxonomy is restricted to eight fixed categories, which, despite being justified for stability, limits the open-vocabulary expressiveness claimed for the overall system and could hide relation-level errors not captured by this coarse taxonomy.

No explicit statement on code/data release, which would be important for reproducibility given the many implementation-specific hyperparameters and prompt engineering choices detailed in the supplementary material.

strengths: The paper targets a genuine and practically important problem: semantic inconsistency in open-vocabulary 3D scene graph construction caused by occlusion and constrained viewpoints during cross-image aggregation.

The core idea of comparing passively-observed captions against captions from a synthetically re-shot 'optimal view' rendered from the fused point cloud is a reasonably novel way to derive a per-object uncertainty signal without extra sensing.

Experimental coverage is broad: two real-world benchmarks (SceneFun3D, FunGraph3D), a carefully designed human evaluation with Fleiss' kappa reported, extensive component ablations (Fig. 3), hyperparameter sweeps (voxel size, merge threshold, scoring weights, RAG top-k), a noisy-pose stress test, and a real robot deployment.

The mechanism-analysis variants (Passive VLM, Re-shot VLM only, Ours Node + CG Edge) help isolate which components drive the reported gains, and the ablation showing failure of isolated re-shooting is informative.
Supplementary material is unusually thorough, including full prompt templates, pseudo-code for object fusion, and qualitative visualizations, which aids reproducibility.
weaknesses: The manuscript cites several works with implausible/future arXiv dates (e.g., 'Think3D' arXiv:2601.13029 (2026), 'Chain-of-View' arXiv:2601.05172 (2026), 'PSG-Nav' arXiv:2606.01313 (2026)) and reports results for a nonexistent model 'gpt-5.2' in Table 1. These anomalies raise serious concerns about citation integrity and the reliability of reported comparisons.

The core 'active re-shot' mechanism only re-renders views from the already-fused point cloud built from the same input RGB-D stream; it cannot recover geometry/appearance that was never observed. The framing as an 'active photographer' that breaks the passive-observation bottleneck is therefore somewhat overstated, since it re-projects existing information rather than acquiring genuinely new observations.

Quantitative gains over the strongest baseline (OpenFunGraph) are often modest (e.g., Edge R@10 97.9 vs 96.2 on SceneFun3D; Edge R@5 65.7 vs 65.1 on FunGraph3D), which weakens the 'new SOTA' framing given the added complexity of the pipeline.

The human evaluation (Table 2) and the real-robot quantitative evaluation only compare against ConceptGraphs/ConceptGraphs-Detector, omitting the strongest automated-metric baseline OpenFunGraph, leaving an important comparison gap.

The injected pose noise for the robustness stress test (σtrans=0.02m, σrot=1°) is fairly small relative to real SLAM/odometry drift, so claims of 'exceptional resilience' may not generalize to more severe real-world tracking failures.

Key design choices (e.g., K=3 for KMeans clustering of similarity scores, the specific similarity threshold δsim=0.45, top-50% low-uncertainty cutoff for the RAG document) are not well theoretically motivated and rely on empirical tuning shown only in the supplementary material.

The system is explicitly offline and computationally heavy (per-object rendering, VLM/LLM calls at multiple stages), which is in tension with the paper's stated motivation of supporting real-time robotics tasks; the robotic deployment itself is a single teleoperated, offline-processed trial.

Absolute performance on the fine-grained semantic segmentation-based ablation metrics (Fig. 3) remains low (e.g., mIoU ~23-24%, mF1 ~30%), suggesting the method, while better than ablated variants, may still be far from reliable for safety-critical downstream deployment as motivated in the introduction.
